obtained.how: Minnesota Legislative Reference Library's copy of the DNR report (the URL in the reference entry)

bibliography.note: Steven M. Shroyer, 'Induced winterkill as a management tool for reclaiming Minnesota walleye rearing ponds', Minnesota Department of Natural Resources Investigational Report 547, July 2007 (Completion Report, Study 603, D-J Project F-26-R)

claims.claim: White suckers died when maximum dissolved oxygen stayed below 1 mg/L for 12 days (killed when maximum dissolved O₂ stayed < 1 mg/L for ≥ 12 d)
claims.quote: remained < 1 mg/L for at least 12 days
claims.conditions: one treated rearing pond (Mortenson Pond, Kandiyohi County, Minnesota), winter 2004, after 'reverse aeration' on 5-6 Feb; 'maximum DO' is the highest DO measured anywhere in the pond (several stations and depths), used because fish seek the best water available; no white suckers were caught in April and the landowner reported many dead white suckers after ice-out
claims.note: the source says 'at least 12 days': ≥ 12 d is the right form. One pond, so it is an observed lethal exposure, not a threshold. Across all ponds the report says winterkill of most species except bullheads and fathead minnows always occurred when maximum DO stayed below 1.0 mg/L for at least six days (p. 30).

claims.quote: Maximum DO in Tatlie Pond only declined to slightly below 4 mg/L
claims.conditions: untreated reference pond, winter 2003-04; adult walleyes and white suckers were caught in April 2004, 'indicating little or no winterkill'
claims.note: again maximum DO (the best water in the pond), one pond

notes: Useful companion values: across the six effective treatments, walleyes, sunfish and white suckers were reduced or eliminated, but black bullhead and fathead minnow populations were never significantly reduced (abstract; p. 30); winterkill of carryover walleyes once occurred with maximum DO of 1.0-2.0 mg/L for at least 14 days (p. 30). The report's ranking (bullheads most tolerant, white sucker among the intolerant) supports the paper's §3.5.6 ordering. The ponds are shallow eutrophic-hypereutrophic Minnesota rearing lakes under snow and ice.
